meta.ogDescription: Credited to Austen’s Emma, but absent from every one of her books. The usual explanation points to a film script.

answer.label: Not Jane Austen — not in any of her books
answer.authorDates: Author unconfirmed · commonly reported as a 1996 screen line
answer.sourceLine: Austen did not write this. We searched the complete Project Gutenberg texts of all six novels — including Emma ↗, the book it is usually credited to — plus Lady Susan and Love and Freindship, and the sentence does not occur; nor does the phrase “perfect for one another” in any form. It is widely reported to come instead from the 1996 film of Emma, written and directed by Douglas McGrath ↗, but we could not obtain a transcript to confirm that, so we report it rather than assert it.

source.excerpt: “Perhaps it is our imperfections that make us so perfect for one another.”
trail: We downloaded the full Project Gutenberg texts of Emma ↗, Pride and Prejudice ↗, Sense and Sensibility, Mansfield Park, Northanger Abbey, Persuasion, Lady Susan and Love and Freindship, flattened the line breaks so no phrase could hide across a line ending, and searched all eight. The sentence is not present in any of them.
Austen’s English Wikiquote page ↗ does not list this line in any section, and a search across the whole of Wikiquote returns no page containing the phrase “so perfect for one another”.

Wikipedia records that the 1996 film of Emma was written and directed by Douglas McGrath ↗ for Miramax, with Jeremy Northam as Mr Knightley, and notes that his screenplay “enlivens the banter between the staid Mr Knightley and the vivacious Emma” beyond the novel. That is the film the quotation is usually traced to; we could not reach a transcript to check the line itself.
source.excerptNote: We cannot show this in context, because there is no context in Austen to show. The word “imperfection” does occur in her novels — eight times across the six — but never in this sentence or anything close to it.
source.rightsNote: No rights badge. Austen’s own writing is long out of copyright, but this sentence is not Austen’s, and we could not establish which work it does belong to — so there is nothing here whose status we can honestly certify. If it is a 1996 screen line, it would be in copyright to the film’s studio.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.heading: About the woman on the graphic
author.bio: Jane Austen published four novels in her lifetime and two more posthumously, and her complete fiction is short enough to search end to end in a few seconds — which is why lines credited to her can be checked properly rather than argued about. She is also among the most-adapted novelists in English, and that is the machinery behind most of her misattributions: a screenwriter writes a sentence in her register, and within a decade it is being quoted as hers.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Austen attracts a particular kind of misquotation — not fabricated from nothing, but written by a screenwriter adapting her, then quietly promoted to the novel. This is the pattern, and her Wikiquote page already documents another instance of it.

items.why: The sentence is absent from the complete text of Emma ↗ and from every other novel she wrote.
Wikipedia confirms McGrath wrote and directed the 1996 film ↗, but we could not obtain a transcript to verify that this line is in it, so we do not credit him on this page.

items.who: Austen, for “a quick succession of busy nothings”
items.why: Her Wikiquote page ↗ records that popular one-liner as coming from a 1999 screen adaptation, rewording a longer sentence in Mansfield Park.

misattribution.truthLine: What we can say for certain is the negative, and it is a strong one: the text of Emma ↗ is freely readable and this sentence is not in it, nor in any other book Austen wrote.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is a well-made sentence, and its cleverness is precisely why it does not read as Austen once you look closely: she was suspicious of that kind of symmetry, and tended to let her characters say it and then be wrong. The line is the moral an adaptation reaches for; the novel is more sceptical.

It is also a useful reminder that a misattribution does not need a villain. Nobody forged this. Somebody wrote a good line for a film, and the credit drifted one step up the chain to the more famous name.
